title: decode-multiplex-handshake-microbench-compendium
body:
Purpose:
This scratch compendium captures small-scale microbenchmarks comparing three decode/ingest strategies under microburst load:
  1) baseline sequential decode (one connection per request)
  2) multiplexed-decoder (shared stream + interleaving responses)
  3) handshake-optimized (lightweight client handshake + warmpath fastpath)

Quick summary (headlines):
- Multiplexing reduces amortized cost per-token at medium sustained QPS (10-40 qps) by ~12-18% vs baseline while slightly increasing p99 in large microbursts.
- Handshake-optimized flow significantly tightens p50/p95 (lower tail) for tiny requests (<= 32 tokens) with modest cost uplift (2-4%) relative to multiplexing, because it reduces connection setup and first-token latency.
- Combined approach (multiplex + handshake warmpath) gives the best dollars-per-1k-tokens for mixed traffic, but requires client coordination and slight runtime routing changes.

Experiment notes (setup):
- Dates: 2028-03-10 to 2028-03-14 (iterative runs)
- Hardware: 2x n1-standard + accelerator types for inference lanes: A100-40GB (core), T4 (edge sim)
- Runtime: redwood-runtime v1.18.3 (local branch multiplex-experiments)
- Models: open-6B-int8 (shortform), open-13B-q4 (longform) — both quantized variants used to simulate different decode costs
- Client harness: jittered Poisson arrival generator, session lengths sampled from production-like distribution (70% short chat micro-turns <= 48 tokens, 20% mid 48-256 tokens, 10% long >256 tokens)
- Measurement intervals: steady-state windows of 300s; microburst injection windows 15s (2x to 5x baseline qps)
- Cost proxy: $/1k tokens estimated from committed price + amortized instance-minutes for A100/T4 (internal sheet referenced)

Workloads tested (short names used in tables below):
- S-Baseline: sequential single-req decode, no connection reuse
- S-Multiplex: single-connection multiplexing, interleaved responses (client ID tagging)
- S-Handshake: handshake-optimized (fastpath for known client tokens + prewarm handshake)
- Mixed: production mix combining above heuristics with routing rules A/B

Key raw numbers (median of 3 runs, p50/p95/p99 in ms for end-to-end first-byte-per-token; qps = successful full requests/s):

ASCII table:
Scenario                     | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | qps  | $/1k tokens
-----------------------------+---------+---------+---------+------+------------
S-Baseline (short-heavy)     | 18      | 120     | 320     | 42   | 1.00
S-Multiplex (short-heavy)    | 16      | 135     | 360     | 48   | 0.86
S-Handshake (short-heavy)    | 12      | 95      | 280     | 46   | 0.92
S-Baseline (long-mix)        | 45      | 280     | 620     | 9    | 1.00
S-Multiplex (long-mix)       | 52      | 300     | 700     | 11   | 0.89
S-Handshake (long-mix)       | 40      | 250     | 610     | 10   | 0.96
Mixed (multiplex+handshake)  | 20      | 140     | 380     | 51   | 0.82

Interpretation notes on numbers: 
- p99 penalties for multiplex occur largely during short 15s microbursts where queueing affects individual long requests (head-of-line). We observed a 10-15% increase in p99 relative to baseline on long-mix bursts.
- Multiplexing increases overall throughput (qps) by ~15% for short-heavy traffic (client connection reuse and batch packing), which drives the lower $/1k tokens.
- Handshake-optimized wins for tiny-turn latency: shaving ~6ms from p50 and ~25ms from p95 in short requests by avoiding TCP/TLS/connection churn and quickly allocating a warmpath slot.

ASCII sparkline: p95 latency over a 5-minute steady run (short-heavy scenario)
[========--===---======--====]  (qualitative: spikes align with injected microbursts at t=40s, 140s, 210s)

Microburst behavior (qualitative):
- At 3x injected qps we see multiplexed lanes absorb bursts better until slot contention for KV cache + attention kernel scheduling causes 1-2x slowdowns for long sessions.
- Baseline encounters more cold-starts and handshake overhead, hurting p50 but sustaining p99 better for long requests because of per-request isolation.

Small table: cost per QPS efficiency (normalized to baseline = 1.00)
Strategy      | tokens/sec per $ | relative efficiency
--------------+------------------+-------------------
Baseline      | 1.00             | 1.00
Multiplex     | 1.18             | 1.18
Handshake     | 1.12             | 1.12
Multiplex+HS  | 1.22             | 1.22

Absolute caveat: our $/1k tokens uses internal amortization (A100 reserved commit assumptions) — if customers run on rented spot/T4-like hardware, multiplex savings look larger (less fixed amortization).

Experiment configuration snippets (how to reproduce quickly):
- Harness command (shortened):
  ./bench/run_client --model open-6B-int8 --pattern poisson --mix short=0.7,mid=0.2,long=0.1 --duration 300 --burst-window 15 --burst-mult 3 --strategy multiplex

- Server config excerpt: (runtime flags)
  --enable-multiplex=true --max-streams-per-conn=64 --kv-prefetch=auto --warmpath-handshake=true --warmpath-timeout-ms=12

Observations and heuristics (operational):
- Tunable: max-streams-per-conn should be conservative for mixed-traffic tenants. We saw a sweet spot near 32 streams for our long-mix runs; above that head-of-line effects increased p99.
- Prefetching KV for frequently requested prompts reduces p50 across the board, but increases memory footprint and can exacerbate cold-slab pressure in multiplexed lanes.
- Admission control: implement a fastpath-exit for long sessions under microburst to prevent long-tail amplification when multiplexing heavily.

Recommendations (short-term):
1) Ship a beta-multiplex flag to selected enterprise tenants for short-heavy workloads; include opt-out for long-session critical tenants.
2) Expose max-streams-per-conn as tenant-level knob and surface a Console heuristic (recommended = 16/32/64 based on observed session-mix).
3) Add a handshaker trace event to request flows so we can correlate handshake time vs first-token latency in our telemetry.
4) Run a 2-week canary with multiplex+handshake on a sample of PLG customers to validate real-world cost impact.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do these savings translate for very small edge GPUs (T4/RTX) running quantized models where attention kernel variance is higher? (need a T4-focused sweep)
- Can we introduce fair-share scheduling inside a multiplexed connection to reduce p99 tail amplification for long sessions? Work with SRE/Serving runtime team.
- Should multiplex be combined with a small per-stream priority field (short-turns get higher priority) — prototype in runtime scheduler.

Pending TODOs (quick):
- [ ] Extract per-tenant cost delta for multiplex beta (ticket INFR-2150)
- [ ] Add warmpath handshake trace + instrument in parity with experiments (owner: Lena)
- [ ] Run T4-only bench and compare with A100 baseline (owner: Ethan)
- [ ] Draft a Console UX microcopy: "Enable multiplex optimization" with tooltip (owner: Product)

Appendix: selected logs / snippets
- Example client log during multiplex microburst: 
  "session_id=abcd123 stream=12 queued_tokens=4 decode_start=17001234 decode_done=17001239 first_byte_latency=14ms"
- Kernel scheduling note: long-session decode tasks occasionally preempted kernel slots; observed ~7% scheduler overhead at peak.

Notes to self: keep this file informal — will extract a one-pager with visual charts for the April infra sync once T4 sweep is done.

References:

End of compendium (draft)
